name: Litecoin
executive_summary: Litecoin launched in October 2011 as one of the earliest Bitcoin forks, built to settle everyday payments faster and more cheaply than Bitcoin while keeping the same proof-of-work security model. In 2019 it added an optional privacy layer called MWEB, letting users shield transaction amounts on the same base chain if they choose to. Its clear strength is institutional access: a live spot ETF, a Nasdaq-listed company holding it as a treasury asset, and formal recognition as a digital commodity from US regulators combine to push its TradFi score to 44. Its clear weakness is security: a real 2026 exploit in the MWEB privacy layer let an attacker forge a large fake transaction, and the response so far has been a patch rather than a full redesign, with no fresh outside audit and no funded bug-bounty program. That unresolved security gap is the main reason the AI-agent-readiness score lands much lower, at 30, since an AI agent transacting autonomously leans even harder on a clean, proven security track record than a human investor typically does.

key_findings: Litecoin clears our regulatory baseline check outright, one of the cleaner cases we've reviewed: a live, physically-backed spot ETF is already trading, and US regulators formally named Litecoin a digital commodity in a joint interpretive release in 2026.

TradFi Approved scores a solid 56, broader institutional access than a mid-tier score alone suggests. Litecoin's live US spot ETF (Canary's LTCC) grew to roughly 214,000-216,000 LTC by autumn 2026, a major European securities depository added Litecoin to institutional custody in 2026, and a Nasdaq-listed company, Lite Strategy, held 751,798 LTC as its primary treasury asset at September 30, 2026 (down from about 833,000 in June as it began writing covered calls and buying back its own shares). Grayscale's older Litecoin trust has refiled to convert into an exchange-listed ETF, still awaiting SEC approval. Each pathway is small in dollar terms next to a fully mature institutional asset, which is why this lands as a solid middle score rather than a top one.

Tokenomics & Supply is Litecoin's strongest category by far at 90. Total supply is capped at 84 million coins, there was no pre-mine or insider allocation at launch in 2011, and roughly 92% of all coins that will ever exist are already in circulation -- monetary discipline on par with Bitcoin's.

Security is Litecoin's clearest weakness, and it fails our baseline security check outright. In 2026, a flaw in Litecoin's optional privacy feature let an attacker forge a large fake transaction, and weeks later a second attempted exploit briefly split the network into two competing chains. Outside services that mistakenly trusted the fake transaction lost real money. The Foundation published a detailed technical post-mortem and has shipped several hardening releases since, and two further critical bugs reported by outside researchers in mid-2026 were fixed before anyone exploited them. But the fix patched the immediate bug rather than redesigning the underlying system, no independent security audit of the current code has been published, and there is still no standing, funded bug-bounty program -- which is why this doesn't clear the bar.

Litecoin also does not currently meet our baseline check for having a real plan against future quantum computers breaking its cryptography. A proposal addressing this was drafted in 2019 but was never finished, and the developer responsible for it has said publicly he doesn't know what a real solution would look like yet.

Privacy & Confidentiality scores 56, a genuinely mixed picture. Litecoin's optional privacy feature is built directly into the core protocol rather than bolted on by a third party, a real structural plus, and its shielded balance has grown past its pre-2026 high. But the very guarantee this feature depends on was broken by a real attacker in 2026, and day-to-day private transaction activity remains thin. Genuine capability and real usage, but a proven security breach in the same feature, is why this lands in the middle of the scale rather than higher.

Real-World Utility scores a weak 20. Litecoin is accepted by several payment processors, but there's no independently verifiable data showing meaningful transaction volume through any of them, and Litecoin's own dedicated payments push from 2018 shut down within months.

On-Chain Health scores 24. Daily network fee revenue is very low relative to Litecoin's market size, even though the number of transactions and active addresses each day remains meaningfully large in absolute terms -- that mismatch between real usage and thin fee revenue is what holds this category down.

Decentralization scores 18. The three largest mining pools control roughly 65-70% of Litecoin's mining power between them, and that concentration was directly demonstrated in 2026 when upgraded mining pools coordinated in real time to reorganize the chain during the security incident described above.

Security Posture is Litecoin's weakest category on the agent-readiness side, at 14, and it's the most heavily weighted category in this framework. The same 2026 privacy-layer exploit described on the investor side is even more consequential here: real money was forged and lost, the fix was a patch rather than a full redesign, no independent security audit of the current code has been published, and no standing, funded bug-bounty program is in place.

Litecoin doesn't offer instant, mathematically final settlement. Like Bitcoin, its confirmations become more certain over time rather than being final the moment they happen -- a structural limitation an AI agent transacting on it would need to plan around.

Execution Layer is a relative bright spot at 50: Litecoin produces a new block every 2.5 minutes, four times faster than Bitcoin, with consistently low and stable network fees (a typical transfer costs a fraction of a cent). The network hasn't been meaningfully congested over the past year, though that also means its true capacity under heavy real-world load hasn't yet been tested.

Composability & Atomicity scores 18. Litecoin has no smart-contract layer, so there's no way for an agent to bundle multiple actions into a single all-or-nothing transaction the way it could on a general-purpose smart-contract chain.

Agent Tooling scores just 10. Apart from read-only data interfaces that let AI tools look up Litecoin activity, there are no Litecoin-specific payment tools, agent wallets, or marketplaces built for AI agents in today's agent-payment landscape, which runs almost entirely on other chains.

KYA (agent identity and compliance) scores 5, near the bottom of the scale. There's no way to cryptographically link an AI agent's on-chain identity to a responsible real-world party on Litecoin today, and because the chain has no smart-contract layer, there's nothing to build that kind of identity system on top of even in principle.

watch_items: Litecoin's Foundation has published a detailed technical post-mortem of the 2026 privacy-layer exploits, but no independent outside audit of the privacy layer or the core software has been published or announced. A published, scoped, current audit would be a direct trigger to revisit the security score on both the investor and agent-readiness sides.

Litecoin has no standing, funded bug-bounty program. In October 2026 the Foundation began raising donations for a Litecoin Core bounty pool, and vulnerabilities are still reported by private email. A properly funded program with published rewards would remove a specific penalty currently applied on both scores.

A 2019 proposal addressing quantum-computer resistance in Litecoin's privacy layer remains unfinished, and Litecoin's creator said in June 2026 he is "not that concerned" about quantum risk. A real plan for the actual signature-forgery risk would be needed to clear the quantum-readiness check.

Grayscale's Litecoin trust (about $82 million) has refiled to convert into an exchange-listed ETF and awaits SEC approval, while Lite Strategy's Litecoin holdings have fallen as it buys back its own shares. Either development is a trigger to revisit the institutional-access score.

Litecoin's core software remains on an older Bitcoin-derived code base and hasn't adopted the wallet-security improvements Bitcoin's software has picked up in recent versions -- worth re-checking at the next reassessment.

No public dataset tracks where Litecoin's mining hardware is physically located or hosted, so that concentration risk couldn't be measured directly -- flagged to re-check if a tracker becomes available.

Litecoin's reliability clock restarted after the April 2026 incident and has run clean since, but its settlement remains probabilistic, which sets a much lower ceiling on the agent-readiness score than the reliability check does.

Two outside protocols that lost funds during the 2026 incident have each since had their own separate security incidents. If their track records improve, or if Litecoin's volume through those cross-chain routes grows, that's worth revisiting on the agent-readiness side.
